title: Mental Maths Addition Grade 2: 6 Tricks Kids Can Do in Their Head + Free Quiz
meta_title: Mental Maths Addition Grade 2: 6 Tricks + Quiz
meta_desc: Six mental maths addition Grade 2 tricks kids can do without paper, from making ten to near-doubles, plus a free 8-question quiz and printable practice.
excerpt: By Grade 2 a child should be able to add two-digit numbers in their head, not on paper. Here are the six mental addition tricks I teach, each with a quick head-maths example, plus a short quiz to test them.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Ask a Grade 2 child what 28 + 9 is and watch what happens. If they reach for a pencil to stack the numbers, they have missed the point of the year. Good mental maths addition for Grade 2 is about seeing that 28 + 9 is just 28 + 10 − 1, and saying ‘thirty-seven’ before the pencil even lands. That is the shift I care about: from writing sums down to holding them in the head and reshaping them into something easier.

This is not the column-and-carry method — that written procedure has its own place and its own lesson. Here we stay entirely in the head. Below are the six tricks I lean on, in the order a seven-year-old should meet them. Each one takes a hard-looking sum and swaps it for an easy one.

1. Number bonds are the foundation of mental maths addition in Grade 2

Before any trick works, a child needs the pairs that make ten — 1 and 9, 2 and 8, 3 and 7, 4 and 6, 5 and 5 — to come out instantly, no counting. They also need the pairs that make the next round number, so 6 + 4 = 10 quietly becomes 26 + 4 = 30. If bonds are shaky, spend a fortnight here and nowhere else. Every later trick is built on this brick.

2. Make ten to bridge through ten

This is the trick that ends finger-counting for good. To add 8 + 5, break the 5 into 2 and 3: give the 2 to the 8 to make a clean 10, then add the leftover 3. So 8 + 5 becomes 10 + 3 = 13. The same move scales up beautifully — 38 + 5 turns into 40 + 3 = 43. A child who bridges through ten never has to dread sums that cross a ten-line again.

Say it out loud first

When I introduce bridging, I make the child narrate it: ‘eight needs two, five gives two, that leaves three, forty-three.’ Speaking the steps keeps them in working memory. After a week the narration goes silent and the answer just arrives.

3. Add the tens, then the ones

For two-digit sums, split each number into tens and ones and deal with them separately. Take 34 + 23: add the tens, 30 + 20 = 50, then the ones, 4 + 3 = 7, then put them together for 57. This partitioning is the single most useful habit for the year because it makes big-looking sums feel small. The one caution: if the ones cross ten, as in 34 + 28, add the tens first (50), then bridge the ones (4 + 8 = 12), then combine for 62.

4. Adding 9 is really adding 10 and stepping back one

Nobody enjoys adding 9 the hard way. So do not — add 10 and take 1 off. For 46 + 9, jump to 46 + 10 = 56, then step back one to 55. Adding 8 works the same way: add 10, step back 2. This is the trick that makes children feel clever, and it is worth pointing out that it is a shortcut, not a different sum.

5. Doubles and near-doubles

Doubles stick in a child’s memory almost like a rhyme — 6 + 6, 7 + 7, 8 + 8. Once they are secure, near-doubles come free. 7 + 8 is just double 7 plus 1. 6 + 5 is double 6 minus 1. Teaching a child to spot ‘these two are almost the same’ saves them counting on again and again for a whole family of facts.

6. Counting on in jumps, not in ones

Counting on still has a place, as long as it is done in useful jumps rather than one finger at a time. To work out 47 + 30, hop three tens — 57, 67, 77 — not thirty little steps. An empty number line drawn in the air, or just imagined, helps a child see the jumps. This is the bridge between counting and true mental calculation.

How to practise without a single worksheet

Mental maths lives in the small gaps of the day, not at a desk. A few things that work with the parents I know:

  • Fire one sum on the walk to school — house numbers are free material.
  • At the shop, ask ‘that is ₹38, how much with the ₹9 pencil?’ and let them use the add-9 trick.
  • Play ‘which trick would you use?’ instead of demanding the answer — naming the method matters more than speed.
  • Keep it to five minutes. Little and often beats a long grind every time.

One honest trade-off: mental maths is slower to show results than drilling written sums, and it can look messier early on. Stick with it. A child who can reshape 28 + 9 into 37 in their head is streets ahead of one who can only stack digits, even if the second child looks tidier this week.

Try the quiz, then the printable practice

The short quiz below tests exactly these six tricks — bonds, bridging, tens-and-ones, adding nine, near-doubles and jumping on. Let your child answer in their head first, then read the explanations together. When they are ready for graded written practice with a full answer key, the printable worksheet at the end has plenty to keep them going.

quiz.title: Grade 2 Mental Addition Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on the six mental tricks: bonds, making ten, tens-and-ones, adding nine, near-doubles and jumping on. Answer in your head, then press Check my score.

questions.q: What is 8 + 6 using the make-ten trick?
questions.explanation: Give 2 from the 6 to the 8 to make 10, then add the leftover 4. 10 + 4 = 14.
Add 10 to get 56, then step back one to 55. Adding 9 is +10 then minus 1.

questions.q: What is 34 + 23 by adding tens then ones?

questions.explanation: 7 and 3 make ten. The bonds to ten are 1+9, 2+8, 3+7, 4+6 and 5+5.

questions.q: 7 + 8 is the same as which of these?
questions.explanation: 7 + 8 is a near-double: double 7 is 14, and one more makes 15.

questions.q: What is 47 + 30 by counting on in jumps?

questions.explanation: Bridge through ten: 2 from the 5 makes 38 into 40, then add the leftover 3. 40 + 3 = 43.

questions.q: A toy costs 26 rupees and a pen costs 4 rupees. How much for both?
questions.explanation: 26 needs 4 to make the next ten, and 4 is exactly what is added. 26 + 4 = 30.

faq.q: Should a Grade 2 child add in their head or on paper?
faq.a: Both, but mental first. Grade 2 is where head-maths for sums within 100 should become the default, with the written column method saved for larger numbers later. A child who reaches for a pencil on 28 + 9 needs more mental practice.

faq.q: My child still counts on fingers. Is that a problem?
faq.a: At this stage, yes, if it is their only tool. Fingers are fine for bonds to ten, but by Grade 2 the aim is to replace them with tricks like making ten and adding nine as +10 minus 1. Give them the better tool rather than banning the fingers.

faq.q: Which mental trick should I teach first?
faq.a: Number bonds to ten. Every other trick — bridging, adding nine, tens-and-ones — leans on knowing the pairs that make ten instantly. Get those solid before anything else.

faq.q: How long should daily mental maths practice be?
faq.a: Five focused minutes woven into the day beats a long session at a desk. Fire a sum on the walk to school or at the shop, and ask which trick your child would use rather than just the answer.
